title: 14 Charged in $22.5 Million Train Cargo-Theft Ring That Allegedly Hit at Least 36 Freight Trains
excerpt: Federal prosecutors say 13 people were arrested Thursday in a 17-count indictment charging a crew with burglarizing at least 36 freight trains across Southern California and stealing more than $22.5 million in Nike sneakers, Milwaukee tools and other goods.
content:
🌎 BEYOND THE 956

Federal authorities say they have broken up a modern-day train robbery crew accused of stealing more than $22.5 million in cargo from freight trains across Southern California — and they say the crew coordinated the thefts through Instagram.

Thirteen people were arrested Thursday morning, November 19, on a 17-count federal indictment charging 14 defendants with conspiracy, theft or possession of interstate railroad cargo, and violence against railroad carriers, according to the U.S. Department of Justice. Prosecutors say the crew burglarized at least 36 freight trains between February 2024 and August 2026, stealing Nike sneakers, Milwaukee tools, electronics and other merchandise and selling it on the black market.

Prosecutors identify 21-year-old Nathan Daniel Angel of East Los Angeles as the alleged leader of the crew. Authorities say Angel and others targeted high-value trains carrying goods from the Ports of Los Angeles and Long Beach, stopped the trains by cutting air hoses, boarded rail cars, and moved the stolen goods to stash houses to sell through fence networks and social media. Prosecutors say the crew used a group chat called “Los Trenes” — Spanish for “The Trains” — to coordinate the thefts, and that Angel filmed himself and two others burglarizing a Nike train in February 2024.

The burglaries happened on railroad tracks in Pico Rivera, Fullerton, San Bernardino and other locations in Southern California, according to prosecutors. The case was investigated by Homeland Security Investigations, the Los Angeles Police Department Commercial Crimes Bureau, the Union Pacific Railroad Police Department and the California Highway Patrol Cargo Theft Interdiction Program, with help from IRS Criminal Investigation.

The defendants were expected to make their first court appearances and be arraigned Thursday afternoon in U.S. District Court in downtown Los Angeles. If convicted, they face a maximum of five years in federal prison on the conspiracy count, and up to life in prison on the violence-against-railroad-carriers counts. An indictment contains allegations only. Every defendant is presumed innocent until proven guilty in court.
